item.dc:creator: Neeraj Dhankher

item.content:encoded:
This week offers a chance to leave emotional confusion behind and start again with more confidence. Romance becomes more stable and affectionate on September 30 and October 1. It could bring more comfort and physical closeness. From October 2, communication accelerates, and curiosity rises. Don’t overthink mixed messages. Weekends ease feelings; 4th October is a good day to bridge the gap, reconnect, or try again on a promising bond.
Zodiac Signs That Need Care This Week
Libra: The first few days may pressure you to quickly respond to someone’s expectations. Don’t agree just to keep the peace. Midweek feels calmer, but communication needs to be more honest by Friday.
Scorpio: Around September 30, a strong attraction can turn into possessiveness. Don’t try to control another person’s choices. Later this week, a confusing conversation might lead to unneeded suspicion if you jump to conclusions before hearing the whole story.
Virgo: When the Moon enters Gemini, expect some surprising romantic developments. You could analyse every message or tone shift. “Allow people enough room to explain themselves instead of making assumptions to fill in the blanks.
Capricorn: Work or practical duties may make you less emotionally available.
Someone close could be looking for more attention, especially toward the weekend. Make sure your seriousness isn't mistaken for a lack of interest.
Zodiac Signs That May Enjoy Good Luck
Aries: A new romantic opening is possible in the first half of the week. Singles might feel emboldened to make a move, and couples can reboot a situation that has recently felt stuck.
Taurus: The heat of attraction is on around 30 September and 1 October. A strong connection may feel more enjoyable. For single people, a more reliable person may take a greater interest.
Gemini: Conversation can build romantic momentum. A casual message, intro or shared interest can quickly turn into something more interesting.
Cancer: The week may end on a softer note. Punarvasu helps emotional repair and renewed trust. Someone from the past could pop back in, or a current bond may feel easier to handle.
Balanced Week for These Zodiac Signs
Leo: Romance is still on, but don’t make every interaction a test of attention.
Sagittarius: You're open to new experiences that may lead to attraction, but not necessarily immediate commitment.
Aquarius: You may have an emotionally interesting friendship that doesn’t need definition just yet.
Pisces: You’re still feeling sensitive, but a little more boundary-setting could help you see the connection more clearly.
Lucky Action of the Week
Clear up an emotional misunderstanding before the week is out. A simple, gentle discussion can help open the door to rebuilding trust and letting romantic energy flow more naturally.

item.content:encoded:
DEAR ABBY: I have a group of friends who get together once a month, usually for a casual dinner. Next month’s gathering will be to celebrate three birthdays, one of which is mine. While planning this gathering (via text), I asked if we could skip exchanging presents and just enjoy our time together. The response from my friends was “No! We’re doing presents.” I know their intention is good; these are very generous friends. But I’m working only part time and have to pay for my health insurance out of pocket. They said I don’t need to get them presents, but they will be getting me presents, so naturally I feel the pressure to reciprocate. While I’m not the most creative person, I could get away with making them something, but I’m also a bit put off. Shouldn’t my wishes have been respected since it’s my birthday? — BIRTHDAY GIRL IN MASSACHUSETTS
DEAR BIRTHDAY GIRL: Happy birthday! Your friends understand why you don’t want to exchange gifts, and they want to give you something anyway. They aren’t doing it to pressure you; they’re doing it out of love. If giving them a handcrafted item would help you feel better, that’s fine, but please don’t feel disrespected by their generosity.
DEAR ABBY: My husband of two years and I are opposites when it comes to planning. He’s spontaneous and acts on the spur of the moment. I’m the type who plans everything down to the last nanosecond (slight exaggeration).
Everything came to a head last Saturday when he suddenly decided to start a household project at 5 p.m. We were supposed to meet another couple for an evening out at 7. When he started the project, I reminded him of our date and asked him to let the other couple know that something had come up and we wouldn’t make it. I thought he had taken care of it until they texted me at 7:15 wanting to know where we were. I texted back, “Been delayed, on my way.” I dressed hurriedly, put on makeup in the car, broke all speed records and arrived there about 45 minutes late. I made excuses for him, knowing he has done this to them before. We were halfway through the meal when he showed up, wearing the same “work around the house” clothes from earlier. (I was surprised the hostess even seated him.) I was embarrassed, the other couple was understandably peeved, and I have had it with his inconsiderate behavior! Please advise. — NOT OK IN OKLAHOMA
DEAR NOT OK: If your husband doesn’t know what a faux pas he committed by leaving the other couple hanging, tell him. His behavior was thoughtless and rude. Because you know he is forgetful, you should have kept asking him if he had made the call, or you could have done it yourself. I think your biggest mistake was trying to cover for him by fibbing. In the future, make sure you arrive promptly. Let him do his own explaining, make his own apologies and experience the fallout.
Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at http://www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.

item.content:encoded:
Miklos on Minnie
What were you hoping for? To take a step outside my comfort zone. To meet the love of my life.
First impressions? Confident, and just as confused as I was about how to start off a blind date.
What did you talk about? The optimal time horizon to plan your life ahead – we oscillated between one and 10 years. After that, I’m embarrassed to admit, loads of K-pop.
Most awkward moment? On my way to the loo I stepped on a dog by accident. I felt horrible, but Minnie assured me it was OK.
Good table manners? The food was so intimidatingly tasty it forced the best table manners out of us. Hers were almost too good, I’d say.
Best thing about Minnie? She is from the best part of town (in my opinion) and it shows. She is unabashedly herself.
Would you introduce Minnie to your friends? They love a bottle of wine. She loves a bottle of wine. There is nothing more to say.
Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian.com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here. What questions will I be asked? We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.
Can I choose who I match with? No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.
Can I pick the photograph? No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.
What personal details will appear? Your first name, job and age.
How should I answer? Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.
Will I see the other person’s answers? No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.
Will you find me The One? We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!
Can I do it in my home town? Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.
How to apply Email blind.date@theguardian.com
Describe Minnie in three words Talkative. Fuzzy. Edgy.
What do you think Minnie made of you? I think she saw me quite accurately: nerdy, but willing to push boundaries and have some fun.
Did you go on somewhere? We did not.
And ... did you kiss? No kissing was had.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I wish I had not stepped on that dog – that’s it really.
Marks out of 10? 9.
Would you meet again? By the end of the date, it was clear to both of us that we were missing a romantic spark … That’s life!
Minnie on Miklos
What were you hoping for? A fun evening.
First impressions? Very lovely guy, good vibes. I was a tad late and he was super understanding. He also noted that he often goes by Mickey, which is pretty funny.
What did you talk about? Travel. Studies. Controversial opinions on music concerts. Katseye (sorry, Miklos).
Most awkward moment? Neither of us could figure out the menu.
Good table manners? Yes, very polite.
Best thing about Miklos? He is super different from me. It was nice chatting with someone who has lived such a different life.
Would you introduce Miklos to your friends? Hypothetically yes, but only as a friend.
Related: Blind date: ‘Bizarrely, she suddenly realised she knew my daughter’
Describe Miklos in three words Intelligent, chatty, inquisitive.
What do you think Miklos made of you? That I was easy to talk to.
Did you go on somewhere? Nope, just headed home.
And ... did you kiss? Couple of hugs, not the vibe for a kiss.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? We both said we would have liked to have been in a different part of town by the canal (the restaurant was lovely though).
Marks out of 10? 7.
Would you meet again? Probably not, but no hard feelings.
Miklos and Minnie ate at the Bull and Last, London NW5. Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

item.content:encoded:
Is Canada’s EU Courtship Realpolitik or Romance?
As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney prepares to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, a question once relegated to the realm of political fantasy is gaining traction in Ottawa and Brussels: Could Canada join the European Union? While full membership remains a legal labyrinth and a political long shot, the surge in dialogue signals a profound strategic realignment driven by transatlantic friction and a shared desire for democratic resilience.
The timing of Prime Minister Carney’s visit is no coincidence. Arriving in Strasbourg on September 16 to speak at the State of the European Union (SOTEU) address, Carney steps onto the stage at a moment when Europe is redefining its security architecture and Canada is seeking to diversify its geopolitical dependencies. Although EU membership is not officially on the agenda, the subtext of the visit is clear: Canada is seeking a deeper, more institutionalized bond with the bloc, potentially exploring models like "associate status" that go beyond traditional trade agreements.
The Legal Labyrinth: Can a Non-European Country Join?
The immediate hurdle to Canadian membership is Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, which states that any "European State" may apply to join. The definition of "European" is both geographic and political. While countries like Turkey and Cyprus have applied despite complex geographic realities, Canada’s location in North America presents a fundamental treaty barrier.
Amending the EU treaties to allow for non-European members would require unanimity among all 27 member states, a politically Herculean task. Furthermore, the EU’s current focus is on internal consolidation and the accession of Western Balkan nations, Ukraine, Moldova, and Georgia. Adding a G7 economy from another continent would require a complete overhaul of the EU’s institutional balance, budgetary contributions, and voting weights.
However, the concept of "associate status" offers a more feasible, albeit undefined, pathway. Unlike full membership, associate status could grant Canada participation in specific EU programs such as Horizon Europe for research, Galileo for satellite navigation, or even aspects of the single market for critical minerals without requiring adherence to the full acquis communautaire (the body of EU law). This model would allow for deep integration without the political toxicity of treaty change.
The Political Driver: Washington’s Unreliability
The primary catalyst for this rapprochement is not necessarily a love affair with Brussels, but a growing estrangement from Washington. Under the second term of President Donald Trump, the US-Canada relationship has been strained by aggressive tariff policies, demands for higher defense spending, and a transactional approach to alliances that unsettles Ottawa.
For Canada, the EU represents a stable, rules-based counterweight to American unpredictability. By deepening ties with Europe, Canada can reduce its economic overdependence on the US, which currently accounts for nearly 75% of its exports. For the EU, Canada is an attractive partner: a stable democracy, a rich source of critical minerals needed for the green transition, and a like-minded ally in the Indo-Pacific strategy.
The discussions around critical minerals are particularly significant. As the EU seeks to decouple its supply chains from China and Russia, Canada’s vast reserves of lithium, cobalt, and rare earths offer a secure alternative. A formalized partnership could see Canadian resources integrated into European battery and tech manufacturing, creating a transatlantic industrial base that is resilient to external shocks.
Beyond Trade: Security and Values
The upcoming talks are expected to cover joint high-tech and security-infrastructure projects, reflecting a shift from purely economic cooperation to strategic alignment. With Europe ramping up its defense capabilities in response to Russian aggression, Canada’s involvement in NATO and its technological prowess in AI and cybersecurity make it a valuable partner.
Moreover, both Ottawa and Brussels are grappling with the rise of authoritarianism and the erosion of democratic norms globally. A closer alliance would signal a commitment to defending liberal democratic values, from press freedom to judicial independence, in an increasingly multipolar world.
A Temporary Flirtation or a New Era?
Skeptics argue that this surge in interest is a temporary response to tensions with Washington, likely to fade if US-Canada relations improve under a different administration. However, the structural shifts in the global economy and security landscape suggest otherwise. The era of unquestioned American hegemony is giving way to a more fragmented world where middle powers like Canada must cultivate multiple strong partnerships.
While full EU membership remains a legal and political fantasy for now, the exploration of associate status and deeper integration is a serious strategic move. It reflects a recognition that Canada’s future security and prosperity are inextricably linked to Europe’s stability and success.
As Mark Carney takes the podium in Strasbourg, he will not be asking for a seat at the table of EU ministers. But he will be laying the groundwork for a new kind of table, one where Canada and Europe sit as equal partners, bound not just by trade, but by shared values, security interests, and a common vision for a resilient democratic order. Whether this leads to a formal union or just a stronger friendship, the message is clear: the North Atlantic bridge is being rebuilt, and this time, it’s being strengthened against the storms ahead.

item.content:encoded:
Your Love Horoscope Is Here For Saturday, September 26: The Aries Full Moon Shows Us The Truth
Your zodiac sign's daily love horoscope is here for September 26, 2026. The Full Moon rises in Aries on Saturday, helping you take stock of your relationship and romantic life.
Not all relationships progress the way you hope, but that doesn’t mean breaking up is your only option. Let the Aries Full Moon reveal what has changed so you can either get your relationship back on track or decide to honor what you deserve from love. It's time to take off any blinders and finally see the truth you’ve been avoiding.
Love horoscopes for each zodiac sign on Saturday, September 26, 2026:
Aries
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Something has shifted within you, Aries. It may feel too tender to understand what it means for your romantic life completely, but on Saturday, it’s important to try.
You aren’t the same person you were at the start of the year or during the New Moon in your sign in April. But even with this Full Moon, the changes aren't over yet. They will keep coming through 2028. Through this process, you will grow in ways you can’t even imagine, so you must make sure your relationship aligns with who you’re becoming.
Taurus
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
A pattern can always be stopped, Taurus. It’s normal to repeat the emotional or behavioral patterns of your childhood or past in your relationships. This is your way of working through the wounds and healing, but it doesn't have to continue.
On Saturday, acknowledge the patterns that exist in your romantic life, even if it means embracing change. You are ready for a love that won’t cause pain.
Gemini
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
You can’t put anyone above yourself, Gemini, no matter how much you love them. This has been the lesson of the Aries lunar cycle. You care about so many people, but learning how to prioritize yourself and your needs is a crucial part of showing up for others.
On Saturday, set the boundaries you’ve been too afraid to put into place. You deserve the same love and care you give to all those in your life. Stop accepting less.
Cancer
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Don't shy away from going after your dreams, Cancer. The Aries Full Moon on September 26 reminds you why it’s always worth it to take action on what you most want.
Whether it’s a particular relationship or a professional dream, you can’t just sit around and wait for everything to come together. Take initiative on Saturday and go after what you want, even if that means changing the course of your life.
Leo
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
In April, the Aries New Moon brought a supercharged era of new beginnings into your life. However, on Saturday, you must pause and use this Full Moon as a review period.
With Neptune and Saturn now retrograde, you can see the truth of any situation as well as the intentions of those in your life. This helps you know without a doubt that you are right where you are meant to be, Leo.
Virgo
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
The truth comes out when you stop trying to control it, Virgo. For you, the Aries lunar cycle has been about surrendering control. When you realize that no matter how hard you try, you can’t actually control the outcome in your romantic life, you’re able to let the universe take over.
Think of nothing but surrendering during the Full Moon in Aries on Saturday. This helps you see people and situations for exactly what they are instead of what you want them to be.
Libra
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
You can’t build a relationship in spite of the truth, Libra. With the surge of Aries energy this year, you’ve been guided to work through several karmic lessons. These may have related to past relationships or even your childhood. However, it’s something that you can’t ignore, no matter how hard you try.
The truth is a requirement for love; otherwise, it ends up being a painful lesson. Hold space for what is revealed with Saturday's Full Moon, knowing the universe has your best interests at heart.
Scorpio
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
You set the tone for what you receive, Scorpio. On Saturday, the Aries Full Moon rises with a surge of personal power as you realize just how much say you actually have over your life and the relationships you choose.
This energy helps you see how you’ve grown and feel greater self-confidence. While you may not have romance on your mind, this Moon also helps you fall in love with your life a little bit more.
Sagittarius
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Trust the process, Sagittarius. Throughout this year, the intense Aries energy asked you to reflect on themes of commitment in your romantic life. That continues now and even after the Full Moon on Saturday.
This energy will ultimately help you choose someone you can build a life with, but you have to trust the universe during this time. This also means trusting your own heart and where it guides you.
Capricorn
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
Do it with heart, Capricorn. Being vulnerable is scary and often inconvenient; however, it is also necessary for love. On Saturday, instead of approaching your romantic life with pure logic or control, do so with your heart.
Prioritize the people you love. Create time to make special memories together and be vulnerable with your emotions. This is the only way to feel the kind of love you dream of.
Aquarius
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
You are always allowed to change your mind, Aquarius. Don't be afraid to undo a decision you previously made. It doesn’t make you flighty or irrational. In fact, honoring the truth and letting that be the reason for change means you’re growing.
You're coming to better understand what you need in your life and from love. You will experience a change of mind during the Full Moon in Aries on Saturday. Be sure you’re honoring it.
Pisces
Photos: NASA & sparklestroke | Design: YourTango
You don't have to be afraid, Pisces. Abundance isn’t simply a passing energy. Instead, it takes root in your life and continues to grow. In many ways, it’s also a lot like love.
Don't be afraid of losing what you currently have. You don’t need to fear that life is getting too good, as this is what you have always deserved. During the Aries Full Moon on Saturday, release your fears and make room for abundance and love.
Kate Rose is a writer, spiritual astrologist, relationship and life intuitive counselor, and bespoke retreat curator.

item.content:encoded:
Ben Affleck may have an Oscar on his shelf, but his kids clearly don't think he's taking home the trophy for relationship advice.
The 54-year-old actor gave insight into his family dynamics with the three children he shares with ex-wife Jennifer Garner: Violet, 20, Fin, 17, and Samuel, 14. His kids aren't pulling any punches when it comes to Affleck's dating life — they are regularly roasting him.
More from SheKnows
Affleck humorously explained on Jimmy Kimmel Live! how his kids mocked him when he tried to share his "lived experience" while they were talking "about their friends and the drama and their relationships" at the dinner table.
"I said, 'You know, well, the thing about that relationship there with that person…'" Affleck recalled. "The 17-year-old [Fin] just turns to me and goes, 'Oh, like you're the expert on relationships?'"
Oops! Those kids are taking note of the Argo star's divorce from Garner in 2018, and his second marriage to Jennifer Lopez, which also ended in divorce in January 2025.
Affleck realized he had become the "caricature" to his kids — he wasn't the "cool dad" he thought he was going to be.
"I, like, give advice or try to talk to them like a parent, as you do … but what I've found is that now it's not only one teenager rolling their eyes," he added. "I catch them giving each other looks."
And of course, you always have to watch out for the youngest one, who seems to have his dad's number.
"We're just browsing around and there's some book by a French guy, and it's called I'm Sorry for Everything, and my kid immediately turns to me, deadpan, and goes, 'Oh, look, Dad, it's your autobiography,'" he said of son Samuel.
Affleck took the ribbing all in stride, and even mentioned how he was "proud" of his son for his comedic chops.
For Affleck, getting teased by his kids may just be the price for trying to dispense relationship wisdom when your own romantic history gives them plenty of material.

item.title: [Cosmopolitan] Experts Want You to Ignore This TikTok Dating Advice That Could Ruin Your Relationship
item.dc:creator: Syeda Khaula Saad
item.description: There is a lot of advice I turn to TikTok for: new exercises for my next glute day, throw pillows that will give my apartment a “fall refresh,” where to buy dupes for expensive makeup. But as a sex and relationships writer, there’s one thing I never take seriously on TikTok: any and all dating advice. Are there some great, qualified relationship experts giving healthy and meaningful relationship advice on TikTok? Of course! Is a majority of the “relationship advice” on the app total and utter ga
item.content:encoded:
There is a lot of advice I turn to TikTok for: new exercises for my next glute day, throw pillows that will give my apartment a “fall refresh,” where to buy dupes for expensive makeup. But as a sex and relationships writer, there’s one thing I never take seriously on TikTok: any and all dating advice.
Are there some great, qualified relationship experts giving healthy and meaningful relationship advice on TikTok? Of course! Is a majority of the “relationship advice” on the app total and utter garbage? Also, yes. And because the latter heavily outnumbers the former, whenever I see someone start talking about how “if he wanted to, he would” I immediately scroll away.
There is this weird phenomenon happening on TikTok where people are encouraged to do no work in a relationship and yet expect a partner that is totally perfect. These fake relationship gurus spout “advice” that doesn’t take into account that we’re humans and that relationships take effort and understanding. Also, we’re all told to essentially expect the worst of the each other, have standards that we, ourselves don’t even meet, and of course, treat every relationship like it’s transactional.
“One of the trickiest parts of going to TikTok for dating advice is that short videos don't allow for complexity and nuance,” Elise Braunschweiger, founder and head matchmaker at Amnity Matchmaking tells Cosmopolitan. “Instead, dating advice gets boiled down to its most controversial, click-baity, and scandalous iteration.”
So we asked the real relationship experts (licensed therapists and psychologists) which TikTok advice everyone would be better off leaving alone.
“Test Them.”
TikTok is constantly telling you to test your partner.
“This can involve things like purposely ignoring your partner, taking a long time to reply to their messages, acting distant, or creating a situation just to see how they react,” therapist Ronald Hoang explains.
While you may think you’re simply trying to figure out how much your partner cares, you’re basically creating more problems in your relationship.
“Instead of encouraging honest communication, it encourages people to play games and expect their partner to figure out what they are thinking,” Hoang says.
Plus, these tests don’t necessarily prove anything. People have different reactions to things, and just because a reaction doesn’t fit perfectly into what you were expecting doesn’t mean your partner doesn’t care for you.
“A healthier approach would be to communicate directly about what you need from your partner rather than deliberately putting them in a situation where they can fail a test they didn’t know they were taking,” Hoang says.
“They Should Automatically Know What You Want.”
Anytime I hear “if he wanted to, he would” my eyes roll so far back into my head I’m afraid they won’t ever come back out again. The problem with this advice is that it encourages people to stop communicating their needs with their partners. Instead, they immediately cast partners off as “inconsiderate” if they don’t meet your needs.
“We've started confusing emotional compatibility with emotional mind-reading,” Rebecca Boone, clinical director says. “Your partner can love you deeply and still misunderstand you, need something different from you, or get it wrong sometimes.”
Instead of punishing our partners for not reading our minds, we should be open to telling them exactly what it is we want and need out of a relationship. If you just keep your mouth shut and wait to see what your partner does, you’re setting your relationship up for failure.
“Any Relationship Friction Is a Red Flag.”
I’ve heard people on TikTok say that “relationships shouldn’t be hard.” And while sure, every day with your partner shouldn’t feel like exhausting physical labor, sometimes being with someone can be difficult—that doesn’t automatically mean you should throw the relationship away.
And yet, TikTok relationship “experts” claim that any little issue is a larger symptom of a bad relationship.
“Not every disagreement is gaslighting, not every need for space is avoidant attachment, and not every uncomfortable interaction means you're in a toxic relationship,” Boone says. “These terms describe real patterns, but when we use them to explain every difficult moment, we can lose the ability to distinguish between a relationship that needs repair and one that is genuinely harmful.”
The reality is that even healthy relationships activate our insecurities sometimes. But it’s about how you navigate communication, accountability, and emotional safety afterward.
“The question shouldn't always be, ‘Did my partner trigger me?’” Boone says. “Sometimes the more useful question is, ‘What happened after I was triggered? Were we able to talk about it, take responsibility, and find our way back to each other?’”
“Be Alert at All Times.”
TikTok relationship advice pushes you to constantly assess and overanalyze your relationship to look for red flags.
“Being overly tuned in to relationship content can create hypervigilance in your relationship,” psychotherapist Ciara Bogdanovic, LMFT says. It can mean that you’re constantly worried about what you deserve, ending up with a “loser,” what you need to fix, and what’s wrong in your relationship.
“It impedes your ability to truly be present in your relationship and enjoy your partner’s company, and instead creates anxiety about whether your relationship is good enough,” Bogdanovic says. “The issues manifest internally as anxiety and externally as arguments and tension with your partner.”
Sure, you should be aware of any concerning behaviors. But if you’re constantly looking for red flags, you’re going to create some on your own. It’s okay to be comfortable in your relationship. In fact, that should be your goal.
“Relationships Are for Financial Gain, Not Romantic Connection.”
I’ll admit, I thought the “sprinkle sprinkle” content was funny—until I realized people were taking it seriously.
Now, people look for different things in relationships. And if you truly are only interested in a partnership for financial support, more power to you (I know how expensive groceries are). But TikTok sometimes pushes the idea that all women should look to men to be providers—and it feels pretty “tradwife” or “manosphere” coded if I’m being honest.
AASECT certified sex & couples therapist Vanessa Cushing says that she understands where this idea comes from: Women often are expected to carry a majority of the emotional labor, household chores, and responsibility of raising children. As a response, people on TikTok have encouraged women to seek out men who at least have money to bring to the table.
“When we get into seeking partners based on what they can provide it creates a dynamic where the relationship becomes transactional,” Cushing says. “Relationships should be about the connection—you know you love someone when you just want to hangout with them. You love their essence—how kind they are how loving they are—not how much they can provide for you.”
While we’d all love to be taken care of, this can be done in more ways than just financially.
“If They’re Not Interested In Sex, Go Cold.”
Apparently there are plenty of people telling men on TikTok that if their partner isn’t interested in sex, they should “let her feel the loss.”
I’m sorry—huh?
I get it, being rejected sucks—which is the feeling these people are monetizing off of.
“A man who’s been rejected over and over finally hears something that makes him feel in control again,” Stephanie Flood, LMFT, says. “Yet, for most women, physical connection follows emotional connection.”
This truly is a manosphere talking point. So let’s get to what you should really do: If you’re noticing that your partner hasn’t been as interested in sex, instead of jumping into defense mode, try understanding what’s happening. Have a conversation. Be open-minded. It could be that your partner isn’t feeling great, they’re super stressed, or you’re just not fostering the emotional connection needed for them to want to be physical with you. “Going cold” will do nothing more than get you closer to a breakup.

item.title: [Bloody Disgusting] 'Tick Fever': New Body Horror Movie In Development Turns Relationship Anxiety Into Bloodthirsty Monsters
item.dc:creator: Meagan Navarro
item.description: Ticks are back in the body horror business with Tick Fever, an absurdist horror movie in development from writer-director Sebastian Granskog and producer Mia Palmgren. “Every Finn has learned to live in fear of ticks since the summers of their childhood. It’s a tiny insect that latches onto your body, breaks through your skin, starts drinking your blood and grows bigger as it takes what it wants from you,” Granskog explained to Variety in a first look that reveals concept art behind the film. Ti
item.content:encoded:
Ticks are back in the body horror business with Tick Fever, an absurdist horror movie in development from writer-director Sebastian Granskog and producer Mia Palmgren.
“Every Finn has learned to live in fear of ticks since the summers of their childhood. It’s a tiny insect that latches onto your body, breaks through your skin, starts drinking your blood and grows bigger as it takes what it wants from you,” Granskog explained to Variety in a first look that reveals concept art behind the film.
Tick Fever was presented at the Finnish Film Affair, which spotlighted similar films with Nordic Lab Genre this year.
Whereas the 1993 Brian Yuzna-produced Ticks saw the parasitic bloodsuckers mutate via steroids, unleashing goopy body horror, Tick Fever is applying a more grounded metaphor.
In Tick Fever, “Years into being together, a co-dependent couple’s relationship starts crumbling due to a suspected tick bite. As Victor spirals into anxiety over his alleged bite mark, Stella pulls away, burying herself in her work. Victor’s anxiety starts manifesting itself as a giant, bloodthirsty tick, pushing the couple further from each other. When Victor notices Stella is also being slowly devoured by a tick similar to his own, he realizes the anxiety and fear keeping them together is the very thing that’s killing them.“
In other words, it’s a body horror film centered on a relationship past its expiration date.
Actors Elias Salonen (“Kalevala: The Story of Kullervo”) and Anna Böhm (“Valhalla Project”) portray the doomed couple in the first concept art for the film, above and below.
Like the ’93 creature feature, Granskog wants to make Tick Fever utilizing practical effects. “As a horror fan, gore has me giggling in my seat when I’m watching a movie. I would love to make this film with practical effects. I hope we can accomplish that, at least mostly,” he tells Variety.
“Sebastian brilliantly balances horror, relationship drama and social satire in this film, and the world he has created is horrifyingly relatable,” Palmgren adds.
Tick Fever is still in active development, so stay tuned for more as we learn it. It certainly sounds as though more horror from Norway is on the way.

item.content:encoded:
Emotions are running high; you will be more introspective and need to be honest about how you feel. Moon in Pisces and Purva Bhadrapada Nakshatra is nearby, so it is intense and serious. If you are single you may be wondering if attraction really runs deep. This can make couples more aware of fears or unfulfilled expectations.
How to Navigate Today’s Energy
Don't romanticise something before you know what it really is. Pisces can make people more sensitive, and Purva Bhadrapada can push people to confront their deeper emotional truths.
Couples need to talk through difficult issues without jumping to conclusions. Singles are often attracted to people with mysterious or intense personalities, but it’s still important to be emotionally available. If you are unsure about something, give it time to become clear. Good chemistry should not replace trust, respect, and consistent behaviour.
Zodiac Signs That Need Care Today
Virgo: You could be too preoccupied with the reasons behind someone’s behaviour. Not all feelings are easy to classify. Let the other person say what they want to say without constantly correcting them.
Gemini: In love, when words and actions are not in sync, it can be difficult to tell what is going on.
Don't fill in the blanks with your own story.
Sagittarius: Your wish for freedom may come into conflict with another's emotional needs. Don’t agree to something that you might later feel is too restrictive, but be clear about what you can offer.
Leo: Someone may want more love or attention from you than they are ready to give. And don’t let their quieter mood affect your worth. Let love be active.
Zodiac Signs That May Enjoy Good Luck
Pisces: Utilise your emotional intelligence to discern when somebody is truly into you. Single people can find someone who understands them on a deeper level.
Cancer: Someone’s kind gesture could make them closer to you. Friendships can develop when both people feel like they can talk to each other without being judged.
Scorpio:
You may find it easier to understand your deeper feelings. Honesty can help strengthen a relationship if you’ve been keeping something important to yourself.
Balanced Day for These Zodiac Signs
Aries: You may be attracted to someone, but you need to control your feelings carefully.
Libra: Taking a light touch when approaching a delicate issue can help to lessen friction.
Capricorn: You’re in a solid relationship, but other commitments may take up your free time.
Aquarius:
You may keep your feelings to yourself until you feel you can trust others more.
Lucky Action of the Day
Today, be honest with yourself and ask yourself one question about love. If you have a clear answer inside, it can help you know what needs more emotional energy.

The strongest approach today is to notice what you feel without immediately acting on every emotion. Sometimes clarity comes not from getting an answer, but from finally understanding why something still matters.

Written by: Tanya Singh of Astropatri.com.

item.title: [Open Magazine] Mindful Intimacy: How mental health affects relationships
item.dc:creator: Gayathri Sreedharan
item.description: Mindful Intimacy: How mental health affects relationships It starts with the ‘partner problem’. We’re taught from a young age that we must find a partner to live out our lives with. item.content:encoded:
Mindful Intimacy: How mental health affects relationships
It starts with the ‘partner problem’. We’re taught from a young age that we must find a partner to live out our lives with. It shapes a deep, sometimes unshakeable desire for one person to be faithful to and intimate with. But what happens to intimacy with another when your internal experience of yourself keeps changing? It’s a dilemma rarely explored on screen. So when I saw that episode of Modern Lovess with Anne Hathaway, evidently living out scenes from my life and proclaiming, “I’m bipolar”, I knew someone understood me.
I was diagnosed with Bipolar II Disorder in late 2018. I’m obviously not alone—India’s National Mental Health Survey data from 2016 suggests that about 0.3-0.5 per cent of India’s population, suffers from Bipolar Affective Disorder (BPAD). I got a diagnosis and started treatment—a 2023 study found that there’s a 70.4 per cent treatment gap among people with current bipolar disorder in India. Honestly, receiving the diagnosis was a relief. I’d had years of prolonged depressive episodes on and off, but I couldn’t explain the manic, hyperactive and hyper-productive stints in between. The diagnosis, paired with a prescription and a treatment plan that included self-compassion, meant I could finally ‘be better’. In 2022, a psychiatrist diagnosed that I had attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms too. I read up on the incidence of bipolar disorder and ADHD occurring in people at the same time, and was surprised to find that it’s not uncommon at all—as of the 2020s, one in 13 adults with ADHD globally can be expected to experience bipolar disorder.
A diagnosis alone, however, doesn’t always lead to addressing challenges with one’s love life. I’ve had therapists and psychiatrists gloss over, even do an eye roll when I bring up romantic conflicts as major triggers. Some of the key conflicts any person with advanced mental health issues can struggle with, such as with self-image, body image, rejection dysphoria, loss of or excessive libido, are all deeply linked with the ability to find and maintain a romantic partnership. Dr Sneha Sharma, psychiatrist and founder of Anvaya Care in the Delhi-NCR region, tells me, “I can’t speak about other psychiatrists… but if [we] are not intentional about understanding the effects of treatment, medication and diagnosis [on interpersonal relationships] then overall wellbeing isn’t being taken into account...a patient might relapse [based on] on how a partner might perceive them, and those factors can precipitate an episode”. If not in the first sitting, the conversation on relationships needs to be intentionally brought forth by mental health practitioners, Dr Sharma insists.
A diagnosis can also sometimes lead to a stalling mechanism, even if inadvertently. Astha Ahluwalia, a Gurugram-based psychologist, says she finds that “for some, dating is postponed with a diagnosis: they think ‘I need to sort my mental health out first’. Sometimes that is genuinely what someone needs, but I wonder whether ‘working on myself’ can also become a safe space over allowing oneself to be vulnerable with another person. Sometimes diagnosis can also become a lens to assess almost every emotional reaction or relationship difficulty… something to hide behind, particularly when accountability and facing our own contribution to relational patterns feels harder”.
Then there’s the crucial challenge of sharing a diagnosis with a partner-in the-making. Ray (name changed), a friend from a BPAD support group in Delhi-NCR, has been adamant in his guidance to me: “Diagnosis is just that; it is not your identity. If you conflate identity and diagnosis, and lead with that, you shut doors to other opportunities.” His advice has always been not to disclose a diagnosis “the first couple of dates”. “Only when things progressed and when it was clear that I could trust the other person, would I share that I live with bipolar disorder. Sites like JeevanSaathi.com were a disastrous experience…the most people could relate to were words like ‘anxiety’ and ‘depression’—dropping the words ‘bipolar disorder’ was like dropping a bomb.”
Ray is now happily married, but he only shared his diagnosis with his wife after a few dates, and she had shared that she sought treatment for depression and was working with a therapist.
I myself have struggled with not sharing. A few months into my treatment, I tried dating during a hypomanic phase. I found myself matching with men who wanted to talk post 10PM, once they were away from the gaze of their prying parents. Treating mental health conditions require sleeping early—not entirely conducive for late night texting. My drowsiness would signal a lack of interest. In my hypomanic phases I’d either excessively crave nothing other than to work long hours, or nothing more than to explore my sexuality. I’d lock in. In both scenarios it would negatively affect my physical health, but also my prospects. When it was the former, I’d forget to eat, hydrate and occasionally medicate, and romantic partners’ appeals to talk or meet would be met with barefaced irritation, or just plain ghosting. In the latter scenario, I’d chase physical intimacy over genuine connections—it sometimes led to connecting with ‘one night stands’ who neither understood nor cared for protection, let alone aftercare. (A 2023 Indian study with a small sample size found that people experiencing acute bipolar depression reported high percentages of sexual dysfunction, up to 91 per cent. Mental health conditions are known to induce both sexual hyperactivity and sexual shutdown, depending on the phase of illness and treatment.)
The highs from both excessive work and excessive dating eventually led me to crash without warning. I’d ghost my paramours again, gladly. When I finally identified the pattern, I decided I would share my diagnosis in dating app bios, and let it serve as a filter. I can’t say whether this decision has paid off or not; Ray, and indeed a few other friends and relatives, have disagreed with this measure. I do know, however, that if I share my BPAD-linked limitations, and the ‘prospect’ cannot or will not understand, perhaps said prospect is not for me.
I’ve had the ‘Anne Hathaway in Modern Love’ days—accidentally having one good look at that face in the mirror is enough to stop all date prep and to sink to the floor for a cry. For many others, the start of the dating process is not the problem. Saket (name changed), who also struggles with BPAD and anxiety, feels “it’s about maintaining the connection”. “The challenges that accompany mental health conditions and treatment mean that I can’t always sustain interest in the process.” The excitement invariably dipping is often brought about by waning moods. It’s not that partners or romantic prospects universally fail to understand mental health blocks. “Most people want to be supportive partners, but they aren’t certain on how to offer support, without neglecting their own needs,” says Pratiksha Tewari, a psychotherapist and learning space specialist at the Hank Nunn Institute (HNI).
Pratiksha and HNI paired up with Sharma and her platform Anvaya Healthcare earlier in 2026 to run a six-part discussion circle, ‘Dil, Dimaag, Dialogue’, which aimed to create a discussion space for persons experiencing mental health conditions as well as their partners. (Disclosure: my own collective, Izaar, helped design and facilitate this series, and I had the opportunity to attend each of these sessions.) “It was surprising to find a mix of regular and new people joining each time, with new inputs to dissect, but there was one repeated, shared concern that stood out for me: participants being in the distressing position of explaining themselves repeatedly… ‘How do I cope? Is it my responsibility to explain, or should it be my partner’s to understand?’ ” Pratiksha says.
Pratiksha also finds that with increasing familiarity with therapy-speak, there’s an increasing use of certain terms or phrases as common parlance, which then find entry into relationship-making and placing responsibility on the other. “People struggle with navigating their relationships around the language of a mental health diagnosis,” she says. (For example, an ex-partner who repeatedly put his indiscretions down to his ADHD, making it tougher to ask for accountability) For Dr Sharma, the main takeaway from the sessions was how important it is to assess relationships during diagnosis: “As a doctor, I have underestimated at times the importance of relational experiences, and the impact it has on well-being, self-esteem, confidence, in relation to how others perceive us. To witness practically how much it affects people has been my biggest takeaway”.
It’s tough to negotiate mental health-speak, even when it’s supposed to induce a modicum of compassion or sympathy, and if possible empathy, in us. No doubt there are a few of us who have figured out how to insist on accountability, and stay genuinely accountable, while also being open with a mental health diagnosis. As for me, having hit perimenopause relatively early, I now find myself even more focused on managing myself over finding someone new. I am now increasingly leaving the dream of an ‘equal partner’ behind, in favour of quiet evenings spent alone or with understanding family and friends instead. It’s not that I’m completely closed off; it’s just that I’ve made peace with and make peace with the ambiguity of what the future holds for a 40-year-old menopausal BPAD woman in India. The more I’ve sought treatment, and the more I’ve conversed with friends, support group members and so on, the more I find I’m secure in not having an answer to the partner problem.

item.description: Taylor Swift drops new single ‘Patient Zero’ about escaping a toxic relationship In 'Patient Zero', Swift appears to address a woman involved with a charismatic but damaging man Taylor Swift has released her new single Patient Zero, a track that explores escaping a toxic relationship and offering support to another woman who may be experiencing the same situation. item.content:encoded:
Taylor Swift drops new single ‘Patient Zero’ about escaping a toxic relationship
In 'Patient Zero', Swift appears to address a woman involved with a charismatic but damaging man
Taylor Swift has released her new single Patient Zero, a track that explores escaping a toxic relationship and offering support to another woman who may be experiencing the same situation.
The 36-year-old singer released the song on Friday, September 25, as the lead single from The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, a surprise expanded edition of her 2025 album featuring four new tracks.
In Patient Zero, Swift appears to address a woman involved with a charismatic but damaging man. Rather than simply reflecting on her own past, the song's narrator tells the woman that she understands what she is going through because she experienced the relationship herself.
Swift describes the man as someone with a "devil on his shoulder under his halo", while using the idea of toxins taking hold to describe the effect of the relationship. She then offers herself as someone the woman can turn to, saying she has already been through the same experience.
The song later makes clear that Swift's narrator had the man before eventually walking away from the relationship. The lyrics centre on recognising harmful patterns, recovering from them and helping someone else who may now be caught in the same situation.
Swift has not publicly confirmed that Patient Zero is about a particular former relationship. However, the song has already prompted fan speculation about which of her past relationships may have inspired its storyline.
The release follows several days of clues from Swift. She changed the "o" letters in her Instagram bio to zeroes, writing, "And, baby, that's sh0w business f0r y0u," before announcing the single following a countdown on her website.
The singer also teased the Patient Zero music video on September 24, revealing that it stars Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell. A 13-second preview aired on CBS Mornings, while the full video is scheduled to premiere during the MTV Video Music Awards on September 27.
Patient Zero is one of four songs featured on The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore. The expanded edition also includes Cleveland!, Pink Clouding and Babylon. Swift said the songs were written during a trip to Sweden with her longtime collaborators Max Martin and Shellback, who also worked on the original The Life of a Showgirl.
The new material comes less than a year after Swift released The Life of a Showgirl, which became a major commercial success. Patient Zero also marks her latest original release following I Knew It, I Knew You, her contribution to the Toy Story 5 soundtrack.
With its focus on toxic relationships, recovery and female solidarity, Patient Zero introduces a different perspective to Swift's latest run of new music while leaving the identity of the relationship at the centre of the song open to interpretation.

item.title: [bostonglobe.com] Blind date: ‘I was genuinely riveted when she told me her horror stories from summer camp’ - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Melissa Schorr
item.description: Go on a blind date. We’ll pick up the tab. Fill out an application at bostonglobe.com/cupid. NATHAN F.: 24 / food service worker/graduate school student What makes him a catch: He’s a tall (6 foot 4), well-read, redheaded musician. Last thing he read: Dubliners by James Joyce CLAIRE S.: 25 / office manager When she is happiest: Sitting in the Boston Public Garden with a book On a desert island, she’d bring: Toothpaste, toothbrush, and floss 8 P.M. PURITAN & CO., CAMBRIDGE Signs to Come Nathan I
item.content:encoded:
Go on a blind date. We’ll pick up the tab. Fill out an application at bostonglobe.com/cupid.
NATHAN F.: 24 / food service worker/graduate school student
What makes him a catch: He’s a tall (6 foot 4), well-read, redheaded musician.
Last thing he read: Dubliners by James Joyce
CLAIRE S.: 25 / office manager
When she is happiest: Sitting in the Boston Public Garden with a book
On a desert island, she’d bring: Toothpaste, toothbrush, and floss
8 P.M. PURITAN & CO., CAMBRIDGE
Signs to Come
Nathan I drove up from a wedding the day of the date. I arrived in time to shower and take the train down. I met a friend and we walked to the spot together, at which point I kindly told him to go find something else to do.
Claire I got ready with my roommates.
Nathan My first impression was, Wow, this girl is short! (She is 5 foot 2.) And then, Woah, she’s dressed kind of badass, because she was rocking a black leather jacket.
Claire He’s very tall! He’s handsome too, and has nice hair.
Higher Power
Nathan We talked about our jobs and where we’re hoping to go in our lives. Turns out, we’re both considering becoming social workers. I was genuinely riveted when she told me her horror stories from summer camp. She also told me she doesn’t listen to music on her commute because she likes to use that time to daydream. I thought that was one of the most interesting things I’d ever been told.
Claire I learned that he was taking a break from divinity school, and that he had been researching substance-use disorders through a spiritual lens. My work relates to mental health, so I was immediately interested in learning more. We spoke about what inspired him to study religion in undergrad and talked about the different religions he learned about. Also, he told me he was in a band, and plays the bass.
Nathan We ordered some grilled zucchini and a large crab cake, and a round of oysters. Later, we got the tuna carpaccio.
Claire The carpaccio was the standout. We also had some champagne and then I tried the Northern Lights cocktail, which was also delicious.
Nathan This first date was noticeably more comfortable than others I’ve been on. We began to tease each other more and care less about what exactly was being talked about.
Claire He’s very easy to talk to. On the way out I grabbed his arm, and we ended up holding hands. It was sweet.
Open Minds
Nathan I was excited to continue the date, so while she washed up I chitchatted with the staff to assess our options.
Claire After dinner, Nathan suggested two bars nearby. I was happy to continue the evening, so we headed to one.
Nathan The date ended with me walking her home. We were pretty happy in each other’s company on the walk back, it seemed to me; I went to give her a little spin at the end of the date and she misinterpreted it, fairly, I think, as a handshake. I was hoping we might feel a little chemistry in that moment, but it didn’t really work out — which is OK!
Claire He offered to walk me home, which I thought was nice. We stood at the corner and chatted for a bit longer, and then we hugged and parted ways.
Second Date?
Nathan I think we will! We have begun chitchatting about it.
Claire I would! I don’t see us running out of conversation topics anytime soon.
Grading the Date
Nathan / B+
Claire / A
Go on a blind date. We’ll pick up the tab. Fill out an application at bostonglobe.com/cupid.

item.content:encoded:
British R&B star Liv East explores modern love on her debut album, ‘FUNKSOULSEX’
25 September 2026
Ahead of her biggest headline show to date at London’s Jazz Cafe on October 8th, British R&B star LIV EAST has released her debut album ‘FUNKSOULSEX’.
Laying groundwork with high-calibre production, intricate instrumentation, and raw, poetic lyricism, East moves fluidly across FUNKSOULSEX.
Exploring themes of seduction, lust, and longing, as well as female autonomy and the romanticised ideals of love, it’s a debut release that affirms her status as a thoughtful, dynamic, and potent voice in British music, navigating love in the 21st century and the blurred lines between desire and fantasy.
Speaking on the album, Liv East explains: “This moment feels like the perfect culmination of years of work, years of creating, years of slowly inching closer to myself sonically and artistically. I’ve always found myself slipping between genres, not out of not knowing myself, but out of never feeling the need to be anything other than what I am. So I decided to create my own genre: ‘FUNKSOULSEX.’ And whatever you feel when you read it, or hear it, is exactly what it is. The holy trinity of funk-infused, soulful, sensual music.”

item.description: DEAR ABBY: I have a mother-in-law of 30 years I distance myself from. I do this in order to maintain my sanity. She seems incapable of carrying on a normal conversation and responds to any comment or question by talking about herself, even though it usually has nothing to do with what was said. item.content:encoded:
DEAR ABBY: I have a mother-in-law of 30 years I distance myself from. I do this in order to maintain my sanity. She seems incapable of carrying on a normal conversation and responds to any comment or question by talking about herself, even though it usually has nothing to do with what was said. What bothers me most is when she’s around our adult children. She won’t ask them any questions, isn’t interested in how they are or what they are up to, and doesn’t say anything loving or kind. Instead, she drones on about other people in her life who have nothing to do with us. We constantly say we don’t know that person, but she continues talking about them. I have tried for many years to redirect conversations, to no avail.
She has been this way for as long as I have known her. Do you think it’s possible to get through to a person like this, to make her understand how a normal conversation should go? Do you think it’s terrible for her grandchildren not to want to be around her? I don’t encourage them to spend much time with her because they end up feeling annoyed and disappointed. That, however, does not sit well with their father. Any thoughts would be appreciated. — FRUSTRATED DAUGHTER-IN-LAW
DEAR FRUSTRATED: Your mother-in-law appears to be solely centered upon herself. If, after 30 years, you haven’t been able to get through to her that her lack of interest in her grandchildren has isolated her from them, you and your husband must recognize that she isn’t going to change. There is no quick fix for this. After three decades of this treatment, your children will never want to be in their grandmother’s presence any more than they are required to be, whether it sits well with their father or not.
DEAR ABBY: My sister and I have an OK relationship. When we were younger, we always fought, but that’s what siblings do. When my father died, I learned about it not from a phone call, but on social media. To say I was hurt and angry is an understatement.
How can I get past this? I told my sister how hurt I was when it happened, but I can’t seem to move on. Now my mother is not doing well, and I’m afraid this will happen again since I have been named executor of her will and a trustee of any assets to be received by my older sister. What are your thoughts on how to get past this and potentially handle any future dealings? — YOUNG EXECUTOR
DEAR YOUNG EXECUTOR: I’m sorry to learn your mother is unwell. Executorship is a big responsibility. As you navigate the next steps, try to set the tone with humility. Instead of dwelling on the past, fulfill your duties objectively and with diligence. If the estate is large and your sister is unhappy with the terms of the will, consult a probate lawyer to keep matters from getting personal.
Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.

item.description: When we dropped by on the sets of Maddy, Rio and Saniya Iyappan were shooting at a cricket stadium. The atmosphere on set was young, fun and relaxed. The cast and crew proceeded to speak to us about the film, which revolves around a man and woman who are complete opposites. It's a jolly, fun-loving story. item.content:encoded:
When we dropped by on the sets of Maddy, Rio and Saniya Iyappan were shooting at a cricket stadium. The atmosphere on set was young, fun and relaxed. The cast and crew proceeded to speak to us about the film, which revolves around a man and woman who are complete opposites.
It's a jolly, fun-loving story. My character, Sachin, studies in a boys' school and concentrates on sports, as his dad (played by Singampuli) wants him to become a cricketer. As a result, he is hesitant to speak to girls. How he finds and interacts with his lover is what the story is about. Although my character’s name is Sachin, Maddy is the name he gives himself. Saniya plays a strong character in the film, which has provided us both equal screen space and performance scope
-Rio, actor
This character is different from the other roles I did in Tamil. It's closer to the real me… someone who travels and is bubbly and modern. I play an influencer. Every heroine has the dream to have a special entry or slo-mo frames for them. In Maddy, you can see me in a proper heroine vibe. When I heard Rio was doing the film, I said, 'I'm in,' because he is an amazing actor whom I like a lot. It's been a fun set. There are nice songs in the film. As a dancer, you wish to dance to good songs, and I got the opportunity in Maddy.
Aju chettan and I haven't worked together in Malayalam. This is our first film together.
-Saniya Iyappan, actress
Rio is a very close friend of mine. I'm happy that I get to play his friend in the film as well. Aju (Varghese) bro is super sweet. BK bro is a young new-generation director. When a team of youngsters come together and begin a startup, there will be a certain kind of energy. That's also the case with this film. Maddy is very close to our heart.
-Vijay, actor
It's a cricket-based love story. It's about what happens when two extremely opposite characters, who are also cricket fans, meet. Basically, it's about a friendly girl and a guy who doesn't know how to speak with girls. Today, the shoot is at a stadium. The heroine is from Bengaluru and is an influencer. Saniya is always on time, and it's been superb working with her. I'm a big Aju Varghese fan. I wrote the role for Yogi Babu, but there was an issue with his dates. I like Aju Varghese sir as much as Yogi Babu, so when we approached him, he also sweetly agreed.
- Karthikeyan BK, director
Maddy is Rio’s biggest film in terms of casting and scale. There's a cricket connection in the film that plays an important factor between the lead characters It's a love story that will connect with boys today with a cricketing and dating app angle. The director wanted Aju, as he felt it would be fresh and unique. I've followed Saniya’s work, and she is the apt choice for the role.
-Kalai Arasu, producer

item.title: [The i Paper] I advise 400,000 women on how to date – this is their most common mistake
item.dc:creator: Harry Hardisty
item.description: The trouble with dating apps is that the carousel never stops. How can anyone make a considered decision about Daisy from Putney when Julia from Richmond is a thumb-twitch away? And somewhere behind Julia, surely, is someone even better. After years of swiping, the patient zero of our interminable romantic misery, the apps, are finally in their death rattle. If they achieved one thing, it’s uniting the world against them. With the apps came dating insanity. I’ve had my fair share. One match popp
item.content:encoded:
The trouble with dating apps is that the carousel never stops. How can anyone make a considered decision about Daisy from Putney when Julia from Richmond is a thumb-twitch away? And somewhere behind Julia, surely, is someone even better. After years of swiping, the patient zero of our interminable romantic misery, the apps, are finally in their death rattle. If they achieved one thing, it’s uniting the world against them.
With the apps came dating insanity. I’ve had my fair share. One match popped up with a gallery of elegant, charismatic photos and a profile Jane Austen could have written. She turned out not to be in her late thirties, as the beautiful prose suggested, but in her mid to late seventies. How did she get away with it? Simple. She’d used her daughter’s photos because, in her words: “I get more matches that way.”
Can’t argue with that. Over the froth of my seemingly never-ending cappuccino, I asked: “But… does it work?” “Oh yes,” she said. “I’ve had loads of fun with younger men.” To be fair to her, the sex was fantastic (kidding). And she wasn’t even the strangest. There was the beautiful woman who took me back to her Surrey mansion, where her husband was waiting in the hallway, in a leather armchair, naked from the waist down.
Apps are a dopamine drip that never runs dry but they don’t actually work because romance was never going to be found by searching. It grows out of attraction and chemistry, one of the few parts of being human that still feels like magic.
I’m not alone in retiring my exhausted digits. In a single year, Tinder, Hinge and Bumble lost more than a million UK users between them. And the people my age who hang on are the most devoted of all. 55- to 64-year-olds on dating apps spend nearly six hours on them in a month, longer than any other age group. That’s a lot of evenings scrolling past partners in crime.
And it’s mostly men doing the swiping: more than six in 10 people using dating services in the UK are male, which will surprise no woman with thumbs. What men get wrong is written all over their profiles. In my work helping people in acute emotional pain, break-up and divorce, I hear from women who are on the apps even in their heartbreak. The relentless draw of the next swipe keeps them chasing the dating app dragon, and they end up drowning in a sea of clichés. If men say they want “no drama, no time-wasters”, they are talking about their last relationship, not hopes for the next one.
Apps are having to adapt too. Tinder has introduced an “events” tab where users can choose to go on real-life dates, from trivia nights to ceramics classes. So, the company that invented “the swipe”, now wants you in a room with other people, making a wonky mug.
These days I give relationship advice to more than 400,000 women on social media. I’ve heard it all: the ghosting, the man who messaged for three weeks and never once suggested a coffee, the profile photos with the ex badly cropped out. I’ve built a whole part of my business offering advice on meeting people in real life.
So, if you’re ready to put the phone down, here’s where I’d start.
Go somewhere more than once. A weekly class, a choir, a walking group, a volunteering shift. The first week you’re a stranger. By the fourth, you’re a familiar face. Attraction often grows out of simply seeing someone regularly.
Choose things you would enjoy even if you met nobody. If the only point of the evening is finding someone, every evening without them is a failure. If you’d happily go anyway, you’re relaxed and better company. Nobody has ever been charmed by someone gritting their teeth through salsa.
Take a friend, then talk to other people. Arriving with someone makes walking through the door easier. Just make a rule before you go in, so you don’t spend the whole evening talking only to each other.
Say yes to the invitations you’d normally dodge. The 50th birthday, the leaving drinks, the barbecue at the house of a friend of a friend. An awful lot of good relationships still start with someone saying: “You must meet my friend.”
If you do stay on the apps, put them in their place. Set a time limit, check them at set times rather than all evening and move to meeting in person quickly. A week of messaging tells you far less than 20 minutes over a coffee.
The swipe had a good run. But it made us fussy, and a little greedy, always sure someone better was one flick away. My seventysomething coffee date understood the game better than any of us: the apps reward the picture, and she’d simply borrowed a better one. The rest of us might do better turning up, again and again, until someone notices.
Harry Hardisty writes about relationships, heartbreak and mid-life at dadhugsforyoursoul.com

item.title: [Yahoo] Libra Season 2026 Love Horoscope: Who’s Dealing with the Drama?
